claims.sentence: The great grammarian changed his mind in print and left the earlier view in his own grammar book, where a reader looking up "gird" would still find Sennacherib.
claims.claim: Radak identifies the earlier Assyrian reading as one he gave under חגר in his Mikhlol.

evidence.quote: כבר במכלול בשרש חגר פירשתי זה המזמור על מחנה אשור ... אבל עתה נראה לי ... לפרש אותו על גוג מגוג

claims.explanation: His retrospective statement establishes the earlier and later readings and locates the former under חגר. “Changed his mind” accurately describes that statement.

claims.sentence: His reason was sequence.
claims.claim: Radak gives the preceding psalm as his reason for preferring the Gog reading.

evidence.quote: אבל עתה נראה לי לטעם המזמור אשר למעלה ממנו לפרש אותו על גוג מגוג

claims.explanation: He explicitly appeals to the psalm immediately above this one.

claims.sentence: Psalm 75 promises a coming judgment, so Psalm 76, he reasoned, must describe it.
claims.claim: The guide’s account of Radak’s sequence-based reasoning is consistent with his reading of Psalm 75.

evidence.quote: כִּ֭י אֶקַּ֣ח מוֹעֵ֑ד אֲ֝נִ֗י מֵישָׁרִ֥ים אֶשְׁפֹּֽט׃
כי ישראל יגדעו אותם במלחמות גוג מגוג
לטעם המזמור אשר למעלה ממנו לפרש אותו על גוג מגוג

claims.explanation: Psalm 75 announces judgment, Radak reads its close in terms of Gog and Magog, and he expressly cites that preceding psalm when changing his reading of Psalm 76. “Must describe it” is the guide’s compressed account of his reasoning, not Radak’s exact words.

claims.sentence: His new reading cost him the forced future tense of v. 3's "and it was."
claims.claim: Radak renders Psalm 76:3’s וַיְהִי as a future event under his Gog reading.

evidence.quote: וַיְהִ֣י בְשָׁלֵ֣ם סוּכּ֑וֹ
ויהי. ואז יהיה בשלם בסכה שיבנה שם בית המקדש

claims.explanation: The contrast between the verse’s “and it was/became” and Radak’s “then it will be” is real. Calling that rendering “forced” is the guide’s assessment.

claims.sentence: Meiri, facing the same fork, lets the reciter choose: the speaker, he says, may interpret it as he wishes.
claims.claim: Meiri allows the speaker to choose an interpretation of the psalm.

evidence.quote: ויתכן לפרשו על מלחמת גוג ומגוג לעתיד והוא הנכון לסמיכותו למזמור שלפניו יפרשם המדבר כרצונו
יש מפרשים שזה המזמור נאמ׳ בנבואה על מלך אשור

claims.explanation: He does end by letting the speaker interpret as desired. The abbreviated account should not obscure his stated preference: he calls the future Gog reading preferable because of its proximity to the preceding psalm.

claims.sentence: It opened with נוֹדָע בִּיהוּדָה, "known in Judah," and closes with נוֹרָא לְמַלְכֵי־אָרֶץ, "awesome to the kings of the earth."
claims.claim: The quoted Hebrew phrases and their translations occur at the opening and close of the psalm’s poetic body.

evidence.quote: נוֹדָ֣ע בִּיהוּדָ֣ה אֱלֹהִ֑ים
נ֝וֹרָ֗א לְמַלְכֵי־אָֽרֶץ

claims.explanation: The superscription is verse 1; the body begins with the first phrase in verse 2 and ends with the second in verse 13.

claims.sentence: The two words differ by a single letter, ד against ר, and the distance between them is the whole psalm's widening from one tribe to the world.
claims.claim: נוֹדָע and נוֹרָא differ by only one Hebrew letter.

evidence.quote: נוֹדָ֣ע ... נ֝וֹרָ֗א

claims.explanation: Ignoring vowel marks, the words are נודע and נורא. Both the third letters (ד/ר) and the fourth letters (ע/א) differ.
claims.suggested_fix: Change “differ by a single letter, ד against ר” to “differ by two letters, ד against ר and ע against א.”

claims.sentence: The last word is אָרֶץ, "earth," its third appearance in five verses.
claims.claim: The last word is אָרֶץ, the third occurrence of that word in verses 9–13.

evidence.quote: אֶ֖רֶץ יָֽרְאָ֣ה ... עַנְוֵי־אֶ֣רֶץ ... לְמַלְכֵי־אָֽרֶץ׃

claims.explanation: The noun אֶרֶץ occurs once each in verses 9, 10 and 13, and closes verse 13.

claims.sentence: On 1 June 1679, an outlawed field-meeting of Scottish Covenanters near Loudoun Hill saw government dragoons under John Graham of Claverhouse riding toward them.
claims.claim: The Covenanter field meeting and Claverhouse’s approach took place near Loudoun Hill on 1 June 1679.

evidence.source: Historic Environment Scotland, Battle of Drumclog inventory
evidence.quote: Arriving at Drumclog on 1 June 1679, having heard that a conventicle was taking place, John Graham of Claverhouse ... found an armed force of Covenanters

evidence.source: Covenanter declaration concerning the June 1679 meeting
evidence.quote: upon the first day of June instant ... captain Graham of Claverhouse ... did furiously assault the people assembled

claims.explanation: The date, field meeting and commander are attested. The declaration also describes the legal threat faced by participants in field conventicles.

claims.sentence: Covenanter tradition remembers that before engaging, they sang Psalm 76 in the Scottish metrical version:
claims.claim: Accounts of Drumclog remember the Covenanters singing metrical Psalm 76 before the engagement.

evidence.source: The Psalms: Their History, Teachings, and Use, account of Drumclog
evidence.quote: When the Covenanters at Drumclog closed their ranks to meet the onset of Claverhouse and his dragoons, they sang the opening verses, to the tune of Martyrs

evidence.quote: waited the coming of the soldiers, singing the seventy-sixth psalm, to the tune Martyrs

claims.explanation: Retrospective accounts support the excerpt’s carefully framed claim about what Covenanter tradition remembers; they do not establish which words every participant sang.

claims.sentence:
> In Judah's land God is well known,
> his name's in Israel great:

claims.claim: The Covenanters advanced against and defeated Claverhouse’s dragoons.

claims.sentence: For these men, persecuted by a king who claimed authority over their church, the psalm's promise that God "prunes the spirit of princes" was a political creed.
claims.claim: The Covenanters faced persecution under a crown that asserted supremacy in Scottish ecclesiastical affairs.

evidence.quote: his majesty hath the supreme authority and supremacy over all persons, and in all causes ecclesiastical within this his kingdom
meeting in houses for divine worship, ministers and people frequently apprehended ... forced ... to attend the Lord’s ordinances in the fields

claims.explanation: The political circumstances are documented. What the particular singers took Psalm 76:13 to mean is the guide’s interpretation, not a separately established quotation from them.

claims.sentence: Every community that has sung Psalm 76 has done what Rashi and Radak did on paper: supplied the missing "we."
claims.claim: Rashi and Radak identify the people delivered in Psalm 76:10 rather than leaving them unnamed.

evidence.quote: לְהוֹשִׁיעַ חִזְקִיָּהוּ וְסִיעָתוֹ
להושיע את ישראל מהם שהם ענוי ארץ

claims.explanation: Rashi names Hezekiah and his company; Radak names Israel. Neither literally inserts the pronoun “we”: “supplied the missing ‘we’” is the guide’s figurative description of their readings.

claims.sentence: The psalm itself never does.
claims.claim: Psalm 76 never uses a first-person pronoun or first-person verb to identify its beneficiaries as “we.”

evidence.quote: נִ֥דְר֣וּ וְשַׁלְּמוּ֮ לַיהֹוָ֢ה אֱֽלֹהֵ֫יכֶ֥ם ... לְהוֹשִׁ֖יעַ כׇּל־עַנְוֵי־אֶ֣רֶץ

claims.explanation: Inspection of the supplied complete psalm shows no first-person pronoun, suffix or verb. It addresses God as “you” and worshipers as “you” plural, while naming the beneficiaries in the third person.
